On an April 2016 royal visit to India, Britain’s Princess Catherine of Wales served up one of the most talked-about fashion moments from her tour, dressed in a pink and blue printed tunic by Anita Dongre , while she played a friendly game of cricket at the Oval Maidan. The cheery, Mughal-print dress caused the designer’s e-commerce website to crash hours later as people flocked to enquire and place orders.
A decade later, on their three-day visit to India for the Earthshot Prize, all eyes were on the Prince and Princess of Wales, eagerly awaiting a similar fashion moment amidst possible theories about which Indian designers they would gravitate towards. The fashion moment soon arrived, this time though from Prince William who threw on a navy blue jacket from Indian handmade contemporary menswear label Kardo over a light shirt and trousers.
The jacket was his pick for a game of cricket at Ballard Estate where he was joined by Princess Kate and cricketing legend Sachin Tendulkar, surprising and delighting fashion watchers with his choice of an Indian label; one that has a story to tell about its commitment to promoting the country’s craft.
Prince William, Princess Catherine of Wales along with Sachin Tendulkar play Gully cricket with youth at Ballard Estate in Mumbai | Photo Credit: EMMANUAL YOGINI
“We have been doing this for over 13 years, and are with at least 150 retailers across the world. But the last few days have truly felt like many more people have woken up to Kardo,” laughs Rikki Kher, founder and creative director of the Noida-based label.
Rikki says that the label made a selection of pieces for Prince William, including contemporary trousers, jackets and suits. “I also decided to make a Nehru jacket; a quintessentially Indian piece which is also contemporary and something that easily translates into a non-Indian setting as well. The silhouette is a representation of our sartorial flair,” he says.
Kardo’s fashion moment, and the subsequent discovery of its brand story by those in India who may have been unfamiliar with its design philosophy and engagement with craft, was perhaps one of the few interesting fashion stories to emerge from the royals’ recently concluded visit to India.
At the Earthshot Prize green carpet, which saw the attendance of several celebrities, notably Bollywood representatives, there was relatively little visibility for brands whose work spotlights sustainability, craft and responsible production. It was a missed opportunity, given the platform the event offered to spark a wider conversation around circularity, fashion’s environmental impact and the ways in which design can be more conscious.
Made of 100% handloom cotton in Harali, West Bengal, Rikki speaks of developing the fabric for the Prince’s Nehru jacket with a team from Glocal Weaves, founded by Fatima Radiowala.
“This fabric is woven on a traditional hand loom in West Bengal using the extra weft technique, where an additional yarn is introduced across the warp to create motifs and patterns, each woven by hand, pick by pick,” he says.
According to Rikki, this extra weft technique was the result of several years of experimentation and refinement since the fabric here needed to accommodate a heavier double-ply cotton yarn. “The result is a fabric that is truly a labour of love, skill and countless hours of work,” he says.
For the Nehru jacket in the news, Netai Mana, Uday Ji and Brojokishore Maity of Glocalweaves from West Bengal have been credited as the weavers, and at the Kardo workshop in Noida, the jacket was hand cut by Jahid Ali and stitched by Virender.
Traditional weaving, dying and printing techniques, as well as fabrics such as natural dyed handloom, block printing, ikat, natural indigo denim, shibori and chikankari embroidery feature in Kardo’s line of menswear through craft clusters from across the country. Rikki speaks of the brand’s commitment to transparency, sharing and community, reflected in how every person who has worked on a garment is credited.
“We also follow a specialised ONExONE production of our clothing where each item is hand-cut, sewn by a single tailor from beginning to end. As a brand that was built with the vision of being the anti-thesis of fast fashion, I wondered how we could go back to the traditional way of making clothes when a tailor was invested and involved in making the whole garment,” he explains.
While Kardo does not call itself a sustainable brand, Rikki speaks of how they work as a low environmental-impact brand and their vision to work in circularity. “When we look at working with an artisanal cluster or group, we want to look at building a long-term relationship. This is not just about working on garments for a single season, but to start small and grow with them. We do not want to create weaves or fabrics that will become unfashionable after one season.”
